blocks.title: 1. Eponyms A-B: Angelman to Briquet
columns: Defining description (as given in the notes)
rows: Congenital mental retardation and epilepsy; distinctive puppetlike movements, compulsive laughter, heritability.
Blindness with denial of being unable to see, and confabulation; a type of anosognosia; classically (not exclusively) bilateral occipital cortex lesions.
Fixation of gaze, neglect of objects in visual surround and misreaching; usually bilateral superior parieto-occipital lesions.

Disorganized hyperactivity (as opposed to waxy flexibility and rigidity in lethal catatonia); can be fatal if untreated; rare, probably because of widespread antipsychotic use; the eponym is antiquated.
A type of multi-infarct dementia (a subtype of **DSM-IV** Vascular Dementia) in which infarcts selectively affect the white matter.
Somatization Disorder; multiple somatic complaints across different organ systems as a manifestation of anxiety.

bullets.text: Angelman syndrome: Congenital mental retardation and epilepsy; distinctive puppetlike movements, compulsive laughter, heritability.
Anton syndrome: Blindness with denial of being unable to see, and confabulation; a type of anosognosia; classically (not exclusively) bilateral occipital cortex lesions.
Balint syndrome: Fixation of gaze, neglect of objects in visual surround and misreaching; usually bilateral superior parieto-occipital lesions.

Bell mania: Disorganized hyperactivity (as opposed to waxy flexibility and rigidity in lethal catatonia); can be fatal if untreated; rare, probably because of widespread antipsychotic use; the eponym is antiquated.
Binswanger disease: A type of multi-infarct dementia (a subtype of DSM-IV Vascular Dementia) in which infarcts selectively affect the white matter.
Briquet syndrome: Somatization Disorder; multiple somatic complaints across different organ systems as a manifestation of anxiety.

blocks.title: 2. Eponyms B-C: Brueghel to Cotard
columns: Defining description (as given in the notes)
rows: Trigeminal dystonia affecting the mouth, sometimes provoked by antipsychotics.
Belief that strangers in disguise have replaced persons known to the patient.
'Global cessation of dreaming'; loss of all or part of dreaming after brain injury.
Visual hallucinations in the context of reduced eyesight.
Any paranoid psychosis in which thought insertions predominate, regardless of etiology.
Congenital mental retardation distinctive for self-injury, hyperactivity, sleeplessness and aggression.
Patient's belief that he does not exist, that part of him (e.g. his organs) is not there, or that he is dead.

bullets.text: Brueghel syndrome: Trigeminal dystonia affecting the mouth, sometimes provoked by antipsychotics.
Capgras syndrome: Belief that strangers in disguise have replaced persons known to the patient.
Charcot-Wilbrand syndrome: 'Global cessation of dreaming'; loss of all or part of dreaming after brain injury.
Charles Bonnet syndrome: Visual hallucinations in the context of reduced eyesight.
Clerambault-Kandinsky syndrome: Any paranoid psychosis in which thought insertions predominate, regardless of etiology.
Cornelia de Lange syndrome: Congenital mental retardation distinctive for self-injury, hyperactivity, sleeplessness and aggression.
Cotard syndrome: Patient's belief that he does not exist, that part of him (e.g. his organs) is not there, or that he is dead.

blocks.title: 3. Eponyms C-G: Creutzfeldt-Jakob to Gardner-Diamond
columns: Defining description (as given in the notes)
rows: Rapidly progressive dementia caused by transmissible prions (proteinaceous infectious particles); distinctive for ataxia, myoclonus, **EEG** triphasic waves and diffuse spongiform appearance of the brain after death.
Panic Disorder; debilitating anxiety attacks accompanied by attempts to avoid such attacks.
Erotomania; more specifically a female patient's belief that a wealthier older man, whom she does not know, loves her.

1) Delusional parasitosis (belief that the skin is infested with parasites, sometimes associated with cocaine use); 2) restless legs syndrome (annoying sensations in the extremities that disturb sleep onset). European physicians prefer the first definition, Americans the second.
Idiopathic calcification of basal ganglia causing dementia and abnormal extra movements, often comorbid with obsessive-compulsive and mood symptoms.
Belief that strangers are actually persons well known to the patient, in disguise.
Symptom of answering all questions approximately, e.g. '2+2=5'.
Purpura associated with psychological stress; subcutaneous injection of the patient's own blood reproduces the rash in the (mostly female) sufferers.

bullets.text: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease: Rapidly progressive dementia caused by transmissible prions (proteinaceous infectious particles); distinctive for ataxia, myoclonus, EEG triphasic waves and diffuse spongiform appearance of the brain after death.
Da Costa syndrome: Panic Disorder; debilitating anxiety attacks accompanied by attempts to avoid such attacks.
De Clerambault syndrome: Erotomania; more specifically a female patient's belief that a wealthier older man, whom she does not know, loves her.

Ekbom syndrome: 1) Delusional parasitosis (belief that the skin is infested with parasites, sometimes associated with cocaine use); 2) restless legs syndrome (annoying sensations in the extremities that disturb sleep onset). European physicians prefer the first definition, Americans the second.
Fahr disease: Idiopathic calcification of basal ganglia causing dementia and abnormal extra movements, often comorbid with obsessive-compulsive and mood symptoms.
Fregoli delusion: Belief that strangers are actually persons well known to the patient, in disguise.
Ganser syndrome: Symptom of answering all questions approximately, e.g. '2+2=5'.
Gardner-Diamond syndrome: Purpura associated with psychological stress; subcutaneous injection of the patient's own blood reproduces the rash in the (mostly female) sufferers.

blocks.title: 4. Eponyms G-H: Gelineau to Hoigne
columns: Defining description (as given in the notes)
rows: Narcolepsy: daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, sleep paralysis, hypnagogic hallucinations, and association with various human lymphocyte antigens.
Finger agnosia, agraphia, right-left disorientation and dyscalculia; associated with dominant parietal lobe lesions.
Transmissible prion disease causing dementia; affects only individuals with particular autosomal-dominant defects of a chromosome.

Interictal behaviour of hyposexuality, hyperreligiosity, hypergraphia and 'viscosity' (not observing appropriate social boundaries in conversation), seen in some patients with chronic temporal lobe epilepsy.
'Periodic catatonia'; a disorganized state of withdrawal or agitation that fluctuates on and off.

Normal pressure hydrocephalus: **CSF** accumulates in the ventricles without a significant rise in intracranial pressure; often causes dementia, gait apraxia and incontinence; shunting reverses the dementia if identified in time.
Childhood Disintegrative Disorder; loss of milestones in multiple domains.
Acute psychosis due to intravenous injection of penicillin.

blocks.forTopic: Gelineau syndrome (narcolepsy) - features listed in the notes
Gerstmann syndrome (dominant parietal lesions) - four features
Geschwind syndrome (interictal, chronic temporal lobe epilepsy) - four behaviours

bullets.text: Gelineau syndrome: Narcolepsy: daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, sleep paralysis, hypnagogic hallucinations, and association with various human lymphocyte antigens.
Gerstmann syndrome: Finger agnosia, agraphia, right-left disorientation and dyscalculia; associated with dominant parietal lobe lesions.
Gerstmann-Straussler-Scheinker disease: Transmissible prion disease causing dementia; affects only individuals with particular autosomal-dominant defects of a chromosome.

Geschwind syndrome: Interictal behaviour of hyposexuality, hyperreligiosity, hypergraphia and 'viscosity' (not observing appropriate social boundaries in conversation), seen in some patients with chronic temporal lobe epilepsy.
Gjessing syndrome: 'Periodic catatonia'; a disorganized state of withdrawal or agitation that fluctuates on and off.

Hakim-Adams syndrome: Normal pressure hydrocephalus: CSF accumulates in the ventricles without a significant rise in intracranial pressure; often causes dementia, gait apraxia and incontinence; shunting reverses the dementia if identified in time.
Heller syndrome: Childhood Disintegrative Disorder; loss of milestones in multiple domains.
Hoigne syndrome: Acute psychosis due to intravenous injection of penicillin.

blocks.title: 5. Eponyms H-L: Hoover to Lesch-Nyhan
columns: Defining description (as given in the notes)
rows: Unconsciously exerted downward pressure with the healthy leg when the paretic leg is challenged; its absence demonstrates a feigned deficit.
Catatonia; waxy posturing or purposeless agitation or speech, treated with benzodiazepines and **ECT**.
Autism; developmental disorder with abnormal communication, impaired social interaction and repetitive behaviour, with symptoms before the age of 3 years.
Hyperphagia, hypersexuality and hypersomnia, classically described in male adolescents.
Temporal lobe damage involving hypersexuality and hyperorality.
Chronic amnesia with difficulty learning new information (anterograde amnesia), manifesting as confabulation; caused by thiamin deficiency; wholly or partially reversible in some cases.
Continuous partial epilepsy leading to progressive cognitive deterioration.
Continuous partial simple epilepsy selectively causing loss of language development in children.
Psychosis without the declining course of schizophrenia.
Congenital mental retardation with defective purine metabolism and ferocious self-injury (the chromosome number given for the deletion in the source is not reproduced here).

bullets.text: Hoover sign: Unconsciously exerted downward pressure with the healthy leg when the paretic leg is challenged; its absence demonstrates a feigned deficit.
Kahlbaum syndrome: Catatonia; waxy posturing or purposeless agitation or speech, treated with benzodiazepines and ECT.
Kanner syndrome: Autism; developmental disorder with abnormal communication, impaired social interaction and repetitive behaviour, with symptoms before the age of 3 years.
Kleine-Levin syndrome: Hyperphagia, hypersexuality and hypersomnia, classically described in male adolescents.
Kluver-Bucy syndrome: Temporal lobe damage involving hypersexuality and hyperorality.

Korsakoff syndrome: Chronic amnesia with difficulty learning new information (anterograde amnesia), manifesting as confabulation; caused by thiamin deficiency; wholly or partially reversible in some cases.
Kozhevnikov syndrome: Continuous partial epilepsy leading to progressive cognitive deterioration.
Landau-Kleffner syndrome: Continuous partial simple epilepsy selectively causing loss of language development in children.

blocks.title: 6. Eponyms L-P: Lhermitte to Parkinson
columns: Defining description (as given in the notes)
rows: Peduncular hallucinosis: bizarre hallucinations (classically visions of Lilliputians) without other psychosis, due to a midbrain lesion.
Dementia due to callosal degeneration, associated with chronic alcohol (particularly wine) abuse.
Palmomental reflex: movement of the chin after stroking the palm; when unilateral suggests frontal or diffuse brain damage.

Fragile X-linked mental retardation due to trinucleotide repeats on the X chromosome; the most common genetic cause of mental retardation; important in psychiatry because many patients suffer from autism and virtually all have attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder.
Dystonic blepharospasm: recurrent involuntary blinking caused by a hypodopaminergic state such as that induced by antipsychotics.
Involuntary muscle fiber activity, hyperhidrosis and sleeplessness leading to death in weeks if not treated; possibly autoimmune.
Glabellar tap reflex: failure to extinguish blinking after 4 taps on the forehead; suggests frontal, diffuse or extrapyramidal disease.

blocks.text: Parkinson disease vs syndrome: the 'disease' is idiopathic degeneration of the substantia nigra causing resting tremor, bradykinesia and rigidity; the 'syndrome' is these symptoms due to some other cause, such as medication.

bullets.text: Lhermitte syndrome: Peduncular hallucinosis: bizarre hallucinations (classically visions of Lilliputians) without other psychosis, due to a midbrain lesion.
Marchiafava-Bignami disease: Dementia due to callosal degeneration, associated with chronic alcohol (particularly wine) abuse.
Marinescu reflex: Palmomental reflex: movement of the chin after stroking the palm; when unilateral suggests frontal or diffuse brain damage.

Martin-Bell syndrome: Fragile X-linked mental retardation due to trinucleotide repeats on the X chromosome; the most common genetic cause of mental retardation; important in psychiatry because many patients suffer from autism and virtually all have attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder.
Meige syndrome: Dystonic blepharospasm: recurrent involuntary blinking caused by a hypodopaminergic state such as that induced by antipsychotics.
Morvan disease: Involuntary muscle fiber activity, hyperhidrosis and sleeplessness leading to death in weeks if not treated; possibly autoimmune.
Myerson sign: Glabellar tap reflex: failure to extinguish blinking after 4 taps on the forehead; suggests frontal, diffuse or extrapyramidal disease.

blocks.title: 7. Eponyms P-S: Pick to Strauss
columns: Defining description (as given in the notes)
rows: Dementia with frontal and temporal atrophy, early personality change and Pick bodies found postmortem.
Congenital mental retardation distinctive for compulsive eating and self-mutilation; caused by a chromosome 15 deletion.
Unilateral brain atrophy and continuous epilepsy resulting in cognitive decline until the affected portion of the brain is removed.

Developmental disorder caused by an X-linked dominant mutation, found mostly in girls: acquired microcephaly, reversal of cognitive and social development, ataxia and hand-wringing (stereotypic hand movements and manual dyspraxia).
Congenital mental retardation caused by a chromosome 12 deletion; distinctive for aggression and insomnia.
Congenital mental retardation distinctive for severe self-injury and 'self-hugging' behaviour.
Dementia with ataxia, loss of ability to look up or down, and parkinsonism.
Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder: inattention and/or hyperactivity, once known as 'minimal brain damage syndrome'.

bullets.text: Pick disease: Dementia with frontal and temporal atrophy, early personality change and Pick bodies found postmortem.
Prader-Willi syndrome: Congenital mental retardation distinctive for compulsive eating and self-mutilation; caused by a chromosome 15 deletion.
Rasmussen syndrome: Unilateral brain atrophy and continuous epilepsy resulting in cognitive decline until the affected portion of the brain is removed.

Rett syndrome: Developmental disorder caused by an X-linked dominant mutation, found mostly in girls: acquired microcephaly, reversal of cognitive and social development, ataxia and hand-wringing (stereotypic hand movements and manual dyspraxia).
Sanfilippo syndrome: Congenital mental retardation caused by a chromosome 12 deletion; distinctive for aggression and insomnia.
Smith-Magenis syndrome: Congenital mental retardation distinctive for severe self-injury and 'self-hugging' behaviour.
Steele-Richardson-Olszewski disease: Dementia with ataxia, loss of ability to look up or down, and parkinsonism.
Strauss syndrome: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder: inattention and/or hyperactivity, once known as 'minimal brain damage syndrome'.

blocks.title: 8. Eponyms S-W: Sydenham to Wolfram
columns: Defining description (as given in the notes)
rows: Movement disorder following rheumatic fever; often preceded by obsessive-compulsive symptoms (first described by Osler), characterized recently as '**PANDAS**' when they occur alone.
Both motor and vocal tics (sometimes coprolalia); often comorbid with obsessive-compulsive symptoms.
Encephalitis lethargica: syndrome that afflicted many victims of a viral epidemic in the early 20th century; distinctive for parkinsonism, lethargy and obsessive-compulsive symptoms.
Triad of delirium, ataxia and abnormal eye movements associated with thiamin deficiency, particularly in alcohol abusers.
Congenital mental retardation with a deletion on chromosome 7; distinctive for fluent verbal ability and an 'elfin' face.

Congenital recessive defective copper metabolism (chromosome 13 defect): hepatic symptoms, later psychiatric symptoms and choreoathetosis. Kaiser-Fleischer rings in the cornea on slit-lamp once the **CNS** is affected (not universally present); more reliable diagnosis is low ceruloplasmin and elevated copper in urine and liver biopsies.

Rare autosomal recessive syndrome from a chromosome 4 defect: diabetes, bilateral optic atrophy and diverse psychiatric disorders. Heterozygotes are extremely common (==1%== of the population) and may be at high risk for psychiatric illness.

bullets.text: Sydenham chorea: Movement disorder following rheumatic fever; often preceded by obsessive-compulsive symptoms (first described by Osler), characterized recently as 'PANDAS' when they occur alone.
Tourette syndrome: Both motor and vocal tics (sometimes coprolalia); often comorbid with obsessive-compulsive symptoms.

Von Economo disease: Encephalitis lethargica: syndrome that afflicted many victims of a viral epidemic in the early 20th century; distinctive for parkinsonism, lethargy and obsessive-compulsive symptoms.
Wernicke encephalopathy: Triad of delirium, ataxia and abnormal eye movements associated with thiamin deficiency, particularly in alcohol abusers.
Williams syndrome: Congenital mental retardation with a deletion on chromosome 7; distinctive for fluent verbal ability and an 'elfin' face.

Wilson disease: Congenital recessive defective copper metabolism (chromosome 13 defect): hepatic symptoms, later psychiatric symptoms and choreoathetosis; Kaiser-Fleischer rings on slit-lamp once the CNS is affected (not universally present).

Wolfram syndrome: Rare autosomal recessive syndrome from a chromosome 4 defect: diabetes, bilateral optic atrophy and diverse psychiatric disorders. Heterozygotes are extremely common (1% of the population) and may be at high risk for psychiatric illness.

blocks.title: Psychotropics adverse-effects chart: effect to drugs
rows: All neuroleptics (less for anticholinergic neuroleptics e.g. **CPZ**); higher-dose atypicals
All antipsychotics, especially thioridazine, pimozide, droperidol

blocks.text: Abbreviations used in the chart: AChEs = anticholinesterases, **BDZ** = benzodiazepines, **CBZ** = **carbamazepine**, **CPZ** = **chlorpromazine**, **VFX** = **venlafaxine**, **VPA** = **valproate**, **SJS** = Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

bullets.text: Extrapyramidal side effects (EPSEs): All neuroleptics (less for anticholinergic neuroleptics e.g. CPZ); higher-dose atypicals.
Seizures: Bupropion, clozapine.
Hepatic damage: Nefazodone, VPA, tacrine.
Weight gain: All antipsychotics (less for APZ, ZPD), TCAs, Li, VPA, CBZ.
Worsening of glaucoma: Paroxetine, quetiapine, TCAs.
QT prolongation: All antipsychotics, especially thioridazine, pimozide, droperidol.
Coarse tremor: Antipsychotic parkinsonism, toxic lithium, valproate.
Haemolytic anaemia: Nomifensine.

mindMap.label: 12. Quick lookup: eponyms regrouped by feature

children.label: Eponyms whose description involves dementia
Binswanger disease: A type of multi-infarct dementia (a subtype of DSM-IV Vascular Dementia) in which infarcts selectively affect the white matter.

Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease: Rapidly progressive dementia caused by transmissible prions (proteinaceous infectious particles); distinctive for ataxia, myoclonus, EEG triphasic waves and diffuse spongiform appearance of the brain after death.
Fahr disease: Idiopathic calcification of basal ganglia causing dementia and abnormal extra movements, often comorbid with obsessive-compulsive and mood symptoms.
Delusions of identity, existence and love; thought insertion
Capgras syndrome: Belief that strangers in disguise have replaced persons known to the patient.
Fregoli delusion: Belief that strangers are actually persons well known to the patient, in disguise.
Cotard syndrome: Patient's belief that he does not exist, that part of him (e.g. his organs) is not there, or that he is dead.
Eponyms whose description involves epilepsy
Angelman syndrome: Congenital mental retardation and epilepsy; distinctive puppetlike movements, compulsive laughter, heritability.

Geschwind syndrome: Interictal behaviour of hyposexuality, hyperreligiosity, hypergraphia and 'viscosity' (not observing appropriate social boundaries in conversation), seen in some patients with chronic temporal lobe epilepsy.
Kozhevnikov syndrome: Continuous partial epilepsy leading to progressive cognitive deterioration.
Eponyms linked to obsessive-compulsive symptoms
Fahr disease: Idiopathic calcification of basal ganglia causing dementia and abnormal extra movements, often comorbid with obsessive-compulsive and mood symptoms.
Sydenham chorea: Movement disorder following rheumatic fever; often preceded by obsessive-compulsive symptoms (first described by Osler), characterized recently as 'PANDAS' when they occur alone.
Tourette syndrome: Both motor and vocal tics (sometimes coprolalia); often comorbid with obsessive-compulsive symptoms.
Eponyms linked to thiamin deficiency

Korsakoff syndrome: Chronic amnesia with difficulty learning new information (anterograde amnesia), manifesting as confabulation; caused by thiamin deficiency; wholly or partially reversible in some cases.
Wernicke encephalopathy: Triad of delirium, ataxia and abnormal eye movements associated with thiamin deficiency, particularly in alcohol abusers.
Eponyms linked to antipsychotics, antipsychotic-like states or other drugs
Brueghel syndrome: Trigeminal dystonia affecting the mouth, sometimes provoked by antipsychotics.
Meige syndrome: Dystonic blepharospasm: recurrent involuntary blinking caused by a hypodopaminergic state such as that induced by antipsychotics.
Hoigne syndrome: Acute psychosis due to intravenous injection of penicillin.
Catatonia, mania and fluctuating motor states

Bell mania: Disorganized hyperactivity (as opposed to waxy flexibility and rigidity in lethal catatonia); can be fatal if untreated; rare, probably because of widespread antipsychotic use; the eponym is antiquated.
Kahlbaum syndrome: Catatonia; waxy posturing or purposeless agitation or speech, treated with benzodiazepines and ECT.
Gjessing syndrome: 'Periodic catatonia'; a disorganized state of withdrawal or agitation that fluctuates on and off.
Developmental disorders of childhood
Heller syndrome: Childhood Disintegrative Disorder; loss of milestones in multiple domains.
Kanner syndrome: Autism; developmental disorder with abnormal communication, impaired social interaction and repetitive behaviour, with symptoms before the age of 3 years.

Rett syndrome: Developmental disorder caused by an X-linked dominant mutation, found mostly in girls: acquired microcephaly, reversal of cognitive and social development, ataxia and hand-wringing (stereotypic hand movements and manual dyspraxia).

mindMap.label: 13. Quick lookup: adverse effects regrouped by drug

children.label: Lithium (Li): Weight gain; Renal damage; Hypothyroidism; Fine tremor (therapeutic dose); Coarse tremor (toxic lithium); Acne, psoriasis.
Clozapine: Seizures; P. ileus; Hypersalivation; Myocarditis / pulmonary embolism; WBC suppression (listed under the '-zapines'); Weight gain and QT prolongation (as one of all antipsychotics).
Valproate (VPA): Hepatic damage; Acute pancreatitis; Weight gain; Coarse tremor; PCOD; Thrombocytopenia.
Carbamazepine (CBZ): Enzyme induction; Weight gain; WBC suppression (listed under the '-zapines'); Rashes, SJS.
SSRIs: GI bleed; Delayed ejaculation or anorgasmia; Sweating; Worsening of glaucoma (paroxetine).
TCAs: Delirium (anticholinergic TCAs); Weight gain; Worsening of glaucoma; Arrhythmias (high-dose TCAs); High BP; Fine tremor; Erectile dysfunction; Sweating; Orthostatic hypotension.

All antipsychotics (as listed in the chart): EPSEs (all neuroleptics); Weight gain (less for APZ, ZPD); QT prolongation (especially thioridazine, pimozide, droperidol); Erectile dysfunction; Orthostatic hypotension; Osteoporosis (hyperprolactinaemic antipsychotics).
